title: Maple and the Sunbeam Chime
markdown:
Maple the raccoon lived under a grand oak in the Whispering Woods. His eyes could spot a fallen acorn from a long way off. His paws could snatch a feather from the air. His den overflowed with smooth pebbles, forgotten buttons that gleamed like tiny moons, and slivers of mica like captured starlight. He spent hours arranging them. A shiny sliver of glass made his chest feel warm. His world was neat, tidy, and full of shine.

The woods hummed. Not only leaves and brook — a soft constant comfort that kept flowers brighter and streams extra joyful. The heartbeat of the forest. Until it stopped.

One morning Maple woke to a gaping silence. The sun still painted dapples on his mossy floor, but the air felt thin and cold. His fur prickled from nose to tail. He wanted to burrow under moss and shiny things. The quiet pressed like a heavy blanket.

“I can’t stay here,” he mumbled to a smooth grey pebble that winked and did not answer.

He poked his nose out. The forest floor, usually alive with scurries and chirps, held still. Every snapped twig sounded huge. A beetle sat on a leaf and did not bother to be busy. Even the brook, when he listened for it, seemed to have forgotten the words to its song.

Maple walked a little way, then a little more. He kept looking back at the oak, at the gleam of his den. The path felt longer without the hum to measure it.

Near a wilting bluebell a tiny spark of light flitted, frantic. Trinket the bell fairy vibrated with distress. Her wings, usually spun-moonlight, looked dull and frayed. Her little bell crown hung silent.

“It’s gone,” she said, voice like cracked bells. “Truly gone.”

Maple edged closer, curiosity shouldering past the shake in his paws. “What’s gone?”

“The Sunbeam Chime. The heart of the woods. Someone’s taken it. Without it the forest will fall asleep. Flowers droop. Paths get lost in the dark.”

Maple’s tummy flipped. He hated the dark. Lost paths sounded like a maze of shadows. He usually stayed put when things got tricky, especially if they involved anything unknown. The thought of the woods going quiet and sad, all their cheerful life fading, was worse than staying in the den with his shine.

Trinket pointed toward tangled brambles. A faint trail of shiny bits glinted. “A clumsy thief. Breadcrumbs. I’m too small for those thorns.”

Maple, who loved shiny things more than almost anything, stared at a path of lost treasures leading toward trouble. He could have scurried home and buried himself in his hoard. He saw the fear in Trinket’s eyes. It looked a lot like his own.

“Don’t worry,” he said, surprising himself. “I’m good at nudging. I have careful paws.”

He eased the brambles aside. A thorn snagged his fur. He winced and pushed on, paw by paw, making a raccoon-sized tunnel where a fairy could never have gone. Trinket perched on his shoulder, a tiny worried passenger, pointing out dropped buttons and lost sequins.

“That’s him. Another one. Oh — a bead like a tear.”

Maple pocketed nothing. The shiny bits were clues, not a collection. That was new for him, and it itched a little, in a useful way.

The trail led to a babbling brook that had found its chuckle again, as if water were braver than air. A bridge of dewdrop pearls spanned it, each drop round and rainbowed. It wobbled at a touch and sang a high delicate note when a dewdrop shifted.

Maple set one paw, then another, on the slippery pearls. The bridge chimed — one note, two, a thin tune that made his whiskers twitch. He wanted to hop and be done. He did not hop. Trinket giggled, a small tinkle that made the crossing a little less unnerving. Midway a dewdrop rolled. Maple froze. The note hung. Then he placed the next paw as if arranging mica at home, where haste spoiled the shine. Together — her light weight, his careful steps — they reached the far bank. The last pearl chimed a thank-you, or something like one.

A gruff voice boomed. “Who goes there?”

A large sleepy badger blocked the path, fur ruffled, eyes squinting, very important nap interrupted.

“He’s always grumpy before his second nap,” Trinket whispered. “We need to sneak past.”

Maple thought of the smooth pebbles in his pouch, the way light liked their surfaces. He flicked the shiniest into rustling leaves behind the badger. Clatter. Jingle. The badger turned, curiosity lumbering after glitter. “What was that?” he grumbled, already halfway into the leaves. Maple and Trinket scurried past, holding their breath until a pine trunk hid them. Behind, the badger muttered about second naps and rude jewelry. Ahead, the trail of shine went on, thicker, as if the thief had grown excited.

The trail thickened — a button, a sequin, a curl of foil like a lost smile. Ancient pines stood like silent sentinels. The air under them was cooler, and the silence here had a shape. On the highest branch, dark feathers ruffled, sat Maredudd the crow. In his beak the Sunbeam Chime pulsed with a faint struggling light, like a trapped firefly.

“Maredudd,” Trinket called, hope and a little fear mixed. “You have to give it back. The woods need it.”

Maredudd cawed, greedy and harsh. The sound bounced off the pines. “Mine. So shiny. Mine.” He loved shine almost as much as Maple. He turned the Chime so a last scrap of sun could live on it. He did not care about the hum or the drooping flowers. He wanted the prize, and wanting was the whole of his plan.

“He won’t listen,” Maple said. The Chime slipped a little in the crow’s beak. “He’s going to drop it.”

Maredudd tilted his head to admire the dazzle. The Chime tumbled — down toward a patch of dark damp moss at the bottom of the grove. The moss looked ready to swallow whatever fell.

Maple’s courage shrank. He always avoided that deepest darkest part. Sticky moss. Shadows. He wanted his den. He wanted not to move.

Trinket tugged his ear. “You’re the cleverest collector I know. Thorns. Bridge. Badger. You can do this.”

He looked at the falling spark. He thought of the silent woods. He would not let the dark have the heartbeat.

He grabbed a handful of his most dazzling pebbles — the ones he had saved for a rainy arranging day — and tossed them high, catching sun. They rained in a sparkling cascade, bouncing, rolling, making a trail of their own.

Maredudd’s eyes locked on the treasures. “Shiny!” He swooped, chasing glitter through the undergrowth, the Chime already forgotten, a black flurry after a brighter one.

Trinket darted, a tiny streak. She hovered beneath the falling Chime. The moss reached. She nudged the Chime from its sticky mouth.

She caught it.

For a moment she could hardly fly for the weight of light. Then the Chime pulsed warm. Shadows leaned back. A soft hum began, faint at first, like someone remembering a tune, then stronger, through trees and earth and air. Bluebells that had wilted lifted their heads. The brook found all its words. Leaves danced. The Whispering Woods had its cheerful heartbeat again.

Trinket landed on Maple’s shoulder, the Chime glowing softly in her hands. Her crown tinkled, just once, as if trying out being a crown again. “Thank you.”

Maple looked at the bright humming woods, then at his paws. He still loved shiny things. He had been scared, and he had still gone. Later they sat by the brook, the dewdrop bridge chiming when a fish kissed the underside. Maple’s den would still hold buttons and mica. A few of his best pebbles were gone into the pine needles for Maredudd to argue with, and he did not mind. The woods, wherever he walked after that, hummed a little brighter, as if it remembered the shine he had thrown away on purpose.
